summary: Built in 1874 on the south side of Hereford Inlet, the light had keepers until 1961; the City of North Wildwood now opens the lighthouse to visitors.

lens.note: Fourth-order Fresnel lens, restored and displayed on the second floor (Friends group).

structures.type: stick-style frame tower on a wooden house
structures.note: 55 feet (NRHP). The Friends group gives 49½ feet; the USLHS record gives 50 feet. The sources disagree.

structures.type: stick-style frame house, integral with the tower
structures.note: Dwelling overhauled and oil house built 1896 (Board report).

access.note: Open daily 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., last tour at 4 p.m., admission free (city site). Visitors climb to just below the lantern room, which is closed to the public (Friends FAQ).

facts.agency: City of North Wildwood (official site). The state held the property from 1964 and leased stewardship to the city in 1982 (Friends).

events.note: Lighthouse Board report recommends a fourth-order light at the entrance to Hereford Inlet (NRHP)
Congress appropriates $25,000 for land and construction (NRHP; Friends gives 10 June 1872)
Site selected; New Jersey legislature grants jurisdiction to the federal government (NRHP)
Construction 8 November 1873 to 30 March 1874 (Friends); built with boat facilities (NRHP)
Notice to Mariners announces the light on 11 May 1874 (Friends)
Fourth-order Fresnel lens (USLHS original optic; Friends)
John Marche appointed first keeper (roster; Friends)
Keeper John March drowned when his boat capsized (NRHP gives 1875; the Friends group and the roster place the death in 1874)
Fixed white light changed to flashing red and white (NRHP). The 1896 Board report says preparations were under way.
Flagstaff erected, telephone installed, signal code flags furnished (Board report; NRHP)

Friends group says a storm in 1913 undermined the foundation and the building was moved 150 feet west. The FAQ dates the storm to September 1913, the history page to August. Not corroborated by the NRHP (which cites landfill) or the Board reports read.
February 1927 storm washes away the beach at Hereford Inlet (Bulletin)
Automatic optic placed on an iron skeletal tower behind the lighthouse (Friends)
Lighthouse closed; the Coast Guard station next door also closed (Friends)
Property transferred to the control of the New Jersey State Marine Police (Friends)
Registered in the state and national registers (newsletter; NRHP 77000859)
New Jersey DEP turns stewardship over to the City of North Wildwood by lease (Friends)
Part of the restored building opens to the public, 1 July 1983 (Friends)
Modern automated light moved into the lantern room and fully functional again (Friends)

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The NRHP says John March drowned in 1875. The Friends group says Marche drowned within three months of starting in 1874, and the roster ends his stint in 1874. Not resolved: the story reports both and marks the year as disputed.
NRHP: tower 55 feet, light 53 feet above water. Friends: 49½ feet and 57 feet. USLHS: 50 feet tower, 53 feet focal height. Not resolved; the story gives the NRHP figure with a note.

The Friends group says a 1913 storm forced the move 150 feet west (dated August in one place and September in the FAQ). The NRHP explains distance from the sea by landfill. No Board report read mentions a move. Not resolved; the story presents the claim as the Friends' and notes the NRHP's explanation.

notes_for_editor: Sources: the NRHP nomination is the chronology base for 1871-1899. The Board's 1896 and 1899 entries corroborate the 1897 change, the 1899 flagstaff and telephone, and the dwelling and oil house work. Friends of Hereford Inlet Lighthouse is a community group site: facts only, own words, the one quotation per claim used as evidence. The Pelz design attribution rests on the Friends site and was not checked against a Board record. The 2017-2018 city takeover rests on The Bay Run (Delaware Bay Lightkeeper Friends, fall 2018), which prints Mayor Rosenello's allegations as quoted claims; no city document was read, so the city's side is only as the newsletter prints it. Newspaper searches for 1875 (John March) and 1925 (Laura Hedges) were attempted, but loc.gov returned HTTP 520 errors, so no newspaper page was read. Ferdinand Heizman: the Board's 1921 Commissioner report names a Ferdinand Heizman as keeper of Great Captain Island (Connecticut), and the 1924-1929 index has 'Heisman, Ferdinand, keeper Great Captain Island'. The Hereford roster names a Ferdinand Heizman from 1926. No source connects them, so there is no other_stations entry. The LSS wreck (November 1883, from the report for the year ending 30 June 1884) is at the inlet and not in the lighthouse's own record; the vessel's name is OCR-damaged and is not used. The 1918-1923 index entry for storm damage at Hereford (p. 117) is cited from the index only; the page text was not found in the local corpus, so its year is unknown and it is not an event. Friends (history) gives the keepers' names with variants: 'Freeling Hysen Hewitt' and 'Robert ONeal 1939-1942' (roster 1939-1945). Record notes: 'status active' is consistent with the city's site; the USLHS place record lists discontinued 1964. Photos not searched.
